clinical_knowledge.topic: Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management follows an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden sharp ear pain, bleeding, and whistling sound when blowing nose after an open-hand slap directly to the ear

Key HPI features: 31M assaulted with open-hand slap to left ear presenting with acute conductive hearing loss, tinnitus, and otoscopy confirming a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the pars tensa managed expectantly with strict water precautions and spontaneous healing over 4 weeks.
Objective/Exam findings: Vital signs stable. Otoscopy shows a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the left pars tensa; no vertigo or facial weakness on exam.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Otitis media with perforation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe vertigo or facial weakness — would suggest a more extensive injury beyond a simple perforation.
management_principles: Keep the ear dry and avoid instrumentation; most small clean traumatic perforations heal spontaneously, while vertigo, facial weakness, severe hearing loss, or persistent perforation requires urgent ENT assessment
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with sudden sharp ear pain, bleeding, and a whistling sound when blowing his nose after an open-hand slap directly to the ear. 31M assaulted with an open-hand slap to the left ear, now reporting acute conductive hearing loss and tinnitus.
reference_soap.objective: Vital signs stable. Otoscopy confirms a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the left pars tensa; no vertigo or facial weakness.
reference_soap.assessment: Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, left ear, confirmed by otoscopy.
reference_soap.plan: Document otoscopic findings and hearing symptoms, keep the ear dry, and avoid ear drops or instrumentation unless specifically indicated. Most small clean traumatic perforations heal spontaneously; arrange audiometry/ENT follow-up. Seek urgent ENT assessment for vertigo, facial weakness, severe sensorineural hearing loss, contaminated injury, or a perforation that does not heal.

Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A sudden pressure change from a slap to the ear tears the eardrum, causing sharp pain, some bleeding, and hearing changes — most small, clean perforations heal spontaneously with water precautions alone.
differentials: Skull base fracture (if more severe trauma)
red_flags: Severe vertigo or facial weakness — would suggest a more extensive injury beyond a simple perforation

must_ask.say: Can you describe exactly what happened to your ear?
How severe was the pain, and did you have any bleeding?
Has your hearing changed since the injury?
Do you notice air or a whistling sound when you blow your nose?
Any dizziness or ringing in your ear?
